About this citation

Written under the pseudonym Vigilius Haufniensis. The book examines anxiety as the dizziness of freedom rather than as a pathology, which is why it is read in philosophy rather than only in psychology.

#### About Søren Kierkegaard

Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855) was a Danish religious author and critic of Christendom who wrote under pseudonyms exploring aesthetic, ethical, and religious existence. Inheriting a melancholy family fortune, he attacked Hegelian system and lukewarm official faith in Copenhagen.

### Interpretation

Kierkegaard compares anxiety to what a person feels looking down from a height: the dizziness comes not from the drop but from the discovery that one could jump. His claim is that anxiety is the experience of possibility itself — specifically of the possibility that one is free. It is therefore not a defect to be removed but the psychological mark of a self with options. This is why he distinguishes it from fear, which has an object, while anxiety's object is one's own freedom.

#### Why it matters

It reframes a familiar feeling: the vertigo before a real choice is not a sign you are unprepared, but the recognition that nothing has settled it for you.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom.”?

“Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom.” comes from The Concept of Anxiety (1844), attributed to Søren Kierkegaard.

#### What does Søren Kierkegaard mean by freedom?

Philosophers distinguish several ideas under the single word freedom. Negative freedom emphasizes non-interference; positive freedom emphasizes the capacity to act according to reasons, virtue, or authentic desire. This passage enters that discussion through freedom, choice.
